claim: Transposable elements (TEs) are mobile genetic elements present in nearly all studied organisms.
source: Transposable elements (TEs) are mobile genetic elements present in nearly all studied organisms, and comprise a large fraction of most eukaryotic genomes.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about TEs.

claim: TEs comprise a large fraction of most eukaryotic genomes.

claim: The two types of TEs are retrotransposons and DNA transposons.
source: The two types of TEs are retrotransposons, which transpose via an RNA intermediate requiring a reverse transcription reaction, and DNA transposons, which transpose via either a cut-paste or, in the case of Helitrons, a rolling circle mechanism with no RNA intermediate (Wicker et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wicker et al., 2007.

claim: Retrotransposons transpose via an RNA intermediate requiring a reverse transcription reaction.
source: The two types of TEs are retrotransposons, which transpose via an RNA intermediate requiring a reverse transcription reaction, and DNA transposons, which transpose via either a cut-paste or, in the case of Helitrons, a rolling circle mechanism with no RNA intermediate (Wicker et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wicker et al., 2007.

claim: DNA transposons transpose via either a cut-paste or rolling circle mechanism with no RNA intermediate.
source: The two types of TEs are retrotransposons, which transpose via an RNA intermediate requiring a reverse transcription reaction, and DNA transposons, which transpose via either a cut-paste or, in the case of Helitrons, a rolling circle mechanism with no RNA intermediate (Wicker et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wicker et al., 2007.

claim: TE activity poses mutagenic potential as a TE insertion may disrupt functional regions of the genome.
source: TE activity poses mutagenic potential as a TE insertion may disrupt functional regions of the genome.

claim: Safeguard mechanisms have evolved to suppress TE activity, including DNA methylation.
source: Consequently, safeguard mechanisms have evolved to suppress this activity, including the methylation of cytosine nucleotides (DNA methylation) to produce 5-methylcytosine (mC), a modification that can induce transcriptional silencing of the methylated locus.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about mechanisms that suppress TE activity.

claim: In Arabidopsis thaliana, DNA methylation occurs in three DNA sequence contexts: mCG, mCHG, and mCHH.
source: In Arabidopsis thaliana (Arabidopsis), DNA methylation occurs in three DNA sequence contexts: mCG, mCHG, and mCHH, where H is any base but G.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about DNA methylation in Arabidopsis.

claim: Establishment of DNA methylation marks can be carried out by the RNA-directed DNA methylation pathway guided by 24 nucleotide small RNAs.
source: Establishment of DNA methylation marks can be carried out by two distinct pathways—the RNA-directed DNA methylation pathway guided by 24 nucleotide (nt) small RNAs (smRNAs), and the DDM1/CMT2 pathway (Zemach et al., 2013; Matzke and Mosher, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zemach et al., 2013 and Matzke and Mosher, 2014.

claim: Establishment of DNA methylation marks can be carried out by the DDM1/CMT2 pathway.

evidence: This is supported by citations to Zemach et al., 2013 and Matzke and Mosher, 2014.

claim: A major function of DNA methylation in Arabidopsis is in the transcriptional silencing of TEs.
source: A major function of DNA methylation in Arabidopsis is in the transcriptional silencing of TEs.

claim: In Arabidopsis, TEs are often methylated in all cytosine sequence contexts, in a pattern distinct from DNA methylation in other regions of the genome.

We found that 89.6% (173/193) of these TE absences were also identified using TEPID, indicating a false negative rate of ~10% for TE absence calls.
